explanations.explanation: Jesus says whoever "climbs in some other way, is a thief and a robber" (John 10:1). Think about that, friend. There's a gate right there, and this guy picks the climbing. That's like sneaking in my bakery window when the front door is sitting there.

The hired hand is a different person in Jesus' picture, and he doesn't show up until John 10:12. The one climbing in some other way gets a harsher name in John 10:1. Jesus calls him "a thief and a robber." So hold that hired hand in your mind, because his turn is coming.

Jesus never calls the climber a shepherd at all. The shepherd is the one who "enters by the gate" (John 10:2). The one climbing in another way is called "a thief and a robber" (John 10:1). I've been the nervous newcomer myself, but even nervous folks use the door.
Jesus says, "the one who enters by the gate is the shepherd of the sheep" (John 10:2). The shepherd walks right in the front. No ladder, no sneaking, no hiding behind a flour sack. Simple as that.

This one is true, friend. Jesus says, "the one who enters by the gate is the shepherd of the sheep" (John 10:2). The climber from the verse before is the one called a thief and a robber (John 10:1). So the gate belongs to the shepherd.

Jesus says the shepherd "calls his own sheep by name and leads them out" (John 10:3). These aren't just any sheep. They're his. And he knows each one well enough to use their name, which is more than I can say for me and the names of my cookie batches.

Jesus doesn't pick out the youngest here. He says the shepherd "calls his own sheep by name" (John 10:3). What matters is that they belong to him, not how old they are. Every one of them gets a name, young or old.

The verse doesn't say a word about sick sheep. Jesus says the shepherd "calls his own sheep by name and leads them out" (John 10:3). The word that matters is "own," and that means they belong to him. Keep your eyes on that word, friend.
Jesus says the shepherd "goes on ahead of them, and his sheep follow him" (John 10:4). He leads, and they trail after. No pushing and no herding from the back. He's up front, and they know it.

That's backwards from what Jesus says. The shepherd "goes on ahead of them, and his sheep follow him" (John 10:4). The sheep are the ones following, so they're behind him. A shepherd at the back would just be a very confused crowd watcher.

No waiting around at the gate in this verse. Once he has brought out all his own, "he goes on ahead of them" (John 10:4). He doesn't stay behind and send them off alone. He walks out in front, and they follow.

Jesus says the sheep "will never follow a stranger; in fact, they will flee from him because they do not recognize his voice" (John 10:5). They don't stop to chat. They're GONE. A voice they don't know is a voice they don't follow.
Not even slowly, friend. Jesus says, "they will never follow a stranger" (John 10:5). Never means never, with no creeping along behind him either. They flee because they don't recognize his voice.

Jesus doesn't say anything about the gatekeeper in this verse. He says the sheep "will flee from him because they do not recognize his voice" (John 10:5). They move away from the stranger on their own. The gatekeeper's job was back in John 10:3, opening the gate for the shepherd.

John tells us the opposite. Jesus used this illustration, "but they did not understand what He was telling them" (John 10:6). I've handed over a cookie recipe and gotten blank stares too. When that happens, you just explain it again, and that's what Jesus does next.
Right, they were lost. John says, "they did not understand what He was telling them" (John 10:6). Jesus doesn't walk away from them, though. He says it again, in a new way, in John 10:7.
Jesus says, "I am the gate for the sheep" (John 10:7). Remember how the shepherd comes in by the gate? Now Jesus says He is the gate itself. Plain words this time, and nothing left to guess.

Close, but that's a different job. The gatekeeper is the one who opens the gate for the shepherd (John 10:3). Jesus says, "I am the gate for the sheep" (John 10:7). He's the gate, not the person standing next to it.
Jesus never says anything about a wall. He says, "I am the gate for the sheep" (John 10:7). A wall keeps things closed, but a gate is where you go in. That's the part He says He is.
Jesus says the opposite. About those who came before Him, He says, "the sheep did not listen to them" (John 10:8). The sheep weren't fooled. They knew a voice that wasn't the shepherd's.

Right, the sheep weren't buying it. Jesus says all who came before Him were thieves and robbers, "but the sheep did not listen to them" (John 10:8). That ties right back to the stranger's voice in John 10:5. The sheep know who they're listening for.

Jesus says, "If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved" (John 10:9). Notice the word "anyone." The gate isn't for a select few. He goes on to say that person "will come in and go out and find pasture."
Jesus doesn't say tested. He says, "If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved" (John 10:9). It's a promise, not a pop quiz. And the same verse adds that he will find pasture.
Counting never comes up in this verse. Jesus says, "If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved" (John 10:9). Saved is the word, friend. I'd take that over a clipboard any day.

Jesus says, "I have come that they may have life, and have it in all its fullness" (John 10:10). Compare that with the thief, who "comes only to steal and kill and destroy." One takes, and One gives. Fullness means the whole batch, not a crumb.

Rest sounds nice, but that's not the word. Jesus says, "I have come that they may have life, and have it in all its fullness" (John 10:10). He's giving something way bigger than a nap. It's life itself.

Shelter isn't the word here, even though we're standing in a sheepfold. Jesus says, "I have come that they may have life, and have it in all its fullness" (John 10:10). Life is what He says He came to give. And He says it comes in all its fullness.

explanations.answer: Lays down His life for them
explanations.explanation: Jesus says, "The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep" (John 10:11). I think this one is heavy, friend, so I'll say it plain. He doesn't only guide the sheep. He gives His own life for them.
Jesus doesn't mention counting. He says, "The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep" (John 10:11). That's a much bigger thing than a nightly check. It's His own life He gives for them.
No gate-building here. Jesus has already said He is the gate (John 10:9). About the shepherd, He says, "The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep" (John 10:11).

Jesus says, "When he sees the wolf coming, he abandons the sheep and runs away" (John 10:12). That's the hired hand, and the sheep aren't his own. When trouble shows up, he's already looking for the exit.

A guard would be nice, but that's not this guy. Jesus says the hired hand "abandons the sheep and runs away" (John 10:12). The wolf comes, and the hired hand leaves. Guarding is the opposite of what the verse says.

Gathering is the opposite of what happens. Jesus says the hired hand "abandons the sheep and runs away. Then the wolf pounces on them and scatters the flock" (John 10:12). The flock gets scattered, not gathered. The hired hand isn't there to gather anybody.

Jesus says, "The man runs away because he is a hired servant and is unconcerned for the sheep" (John 10:13). The sheep aren't his own, and he doesn't care about them. When your heart isn't in the batch, you don't stick around for the burnt part. That's the big difference between him and the good shepherd.

This one is true, friend. Jesus says the man runs away "because he is a hired servant and is unconcerned for the sheep" (John 10:13). The reason is right there in the verse. He doesn't care about the sheep.

Jesus says, "I know My sheep and My sheep know Me, just as the Father knows Me and I know the Father" (John 10:14-15). Let that sink in. He's comparing it to how He and the Father know each other. That's no casual hello at the gate.
It's true, friend. Jesus says, "I know My sheep and My sheep know Me, just as the Father knows Me and I know the Father" (John 10:14-15). He puts the two side by side. It's a deep kind of knowing.

Jesus says of His other sheep, "they will listen to My voice" (John 10:16). Voice has been the word all the way through this picture. Back in John 10:4 the sheep follow the shepherd because they know his voice. Same idea, and it covers sheep who aren't in this fold yet.
Warnings isn't the word Jesus uses. He says, "they will listen to My voice" (John 10:16). It's His voice they listen to, the same voice the sheep know from John 10:4.

Good guess, since Jesus makes plenty of promises, but this verse says something else. He says of the other sheep, "they will listen to My voice" (John 10:16). Voice is the word. It's what the sheep listen for all through the picture.

Jesus says, "Then there will be one flock and one shepherd" (John 10:16). He has sheep that are not of this fold, and He must bring them in as well. When He does, it all becomes one flock. One flock and one shepherd, friend.

Jesus doesn't leave it at two. He says the other sheep will listen to His voice, "Then there will be one flock and one shepherd" (John 10:16). Not two flocks sharing a shepherd. They come together as one.
That's not how Jesus puts it. He says, "Then there will be one flock and one shepherd" (John 10:16). Not side by side, but together as one flock. And there's only one shepherd leading them.

Jesus says, "I lay down My life in order to take it up again" (John 10:17). Laying it down isn't the end of the sentence. He says it's so He can take it up again. I'll let His words stand just as He said them.
Jesus doesn't say that. He says, "I lay down My life in order to take it up again" (John 10:17). He says He takes it up again, so He isn't leaving the flock forever. That's the purpose He names.

explanations.answer: To rest from all His work
explanations.explanation: Rest isn't the purpose Jesus gives. He says, "I lay down My life in order to take it up again" (John 10:17). The purpose He names is taking it up again. No other reason is given in this verse.

Jesus says the opposite: "No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord" (John 10:18). Nobody snatches it away from Him. He says He has "authority to lay it down and authority to take it up again." And He says He received this charge from His Father.

That's right. Jesus says, "No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord" (John 10:18). He also says He has authority to lay it down and to take it up again. It's a charge He received from His Father.

explanations.answer: A demon can't open blind eyes
explanations.explanation: The others say, "These are not the words of a man possessed by a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?" (John 10:21). They're pointing at what just happened with the man born blind. A question like that is hard to argue with.
That's not what they point to. In John 10:21 the others say, "Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?" Their argument is about the opening of blind eyes. Nothing in this verse mentions Sabbath rules.

explanations.answer: The Pharisees all agree with Him
explanations.explanation: Nobody says that here. John tells us "there was division among the Jews because of Jesus' message" (John 10:19). The others answer with a question, "Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?" (John 10:21). That's what they point to.
